title: India's Brain Health Crisis Deepens as Neurologist Shortage Leaves Millions Without Care
excerpt: With 80 times fewer neurologists per capita than wealthy nations and 3.5 million new cases of neurological disability each year, India's growing brain disorder burden is straining an already overstretched healthcare system.
body:
• India's neurologist-to-patient ratio is nearly 80 times worse than that of high-income nations, according to the WHO's 2025 Global Status Report on Neurology.
  • Brain injuries, stroke, and age-related dementia together produce 3.5 million new cases of neurological disability in India every year — roughly 11,000 per day.
  • Most neurologists are concentrated in Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru, leaving vast rural regions as "neurology deserts" with virtually no specialist access.
  • World Brain Day on July 22 is spotlighting the crisis, with calls for decentralized care models and tele-neurology networks.

A Growing Burden

Neurological disorders have become one of India's most pressing — and most overlooked — public health challenges. A 2025 WHO report found that more than 40 percent of the global population lives with a neurological condition, and India carries a disproportionate share of that burden. Mortality from neurological diseases in the country has climbed from 21.01 to 24.27 per 100,000 people over the past three decades, according to a Global Burden of Disease analysis of BRICS nations published in Frontiers in Neurology.

The numbers are staggering. Traumatic brain injury, stroke, and age-related dementia together account for more than 3.5 million new cases of neurological disability each year in India — roughly 11,000 every day, or seven people every minute, according to joint research by the Kessler Foundation and the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences.

The Neurologist Desert

The crisis is as much about access as it is about prevalence. India's neurologist-to-patient ratio is nearly 80 times worse than that of high-income nations, the WHO report noted. Most of the country's neurologists are clustered in metropolitan centers like Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru, leaving smaller cities, towns, and rural districts with little or no specialist coverage.

For patients outside these urban hubs, seeing a neurologist often means long-distance travel, extended waits, or settling for non-specialist care from general practitioners who may lack the training to diagnose complex neurological conditions. Delayed intervention in conditions like stroke, epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, and dementia can lead to preventable disability.

"Because of the uneven distribution of wealth and health care, the rural poor are disproportionately affected. Lack of awareness and stigma associated with disability contribute to the problem."

— Dr. Kurupath Radhakrishnan, Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences

A Policy Gap

The WHO found that only 32 percent of its member states — 63 countries — have a national policy addressing neurological disorders, and just 18 percent have dedicated funding for them. India, despite the scale of its neurological burden, has yet to implement a comprehensive standalone neurology policy at the national level, although initiatives by NITI Aayog and the Ministry of Health have acknowledged the growing problem.

Dr. Vinod Paul, then a member of NITI Aayog, noted that while government policies exist, "more focused efforts are required for the planning of specific neurology services in each state," including addressing the trained workforce shortage and strengthening early detection.

Technology and Decentralization

Experts argue the solution lies in decentralizing neurological care rather than expanding urban tertiary centers alone. Tele-neurology networks, structured referral partnerships, and home-monitoring technologies — including wearable fall-detection systems for the elderly — could bring specialist expertise closer to where patients live.

Falls among the elderly, often dismissed as isolated incidents, can be among the earliest indicators of Parkinson's disease, stroke-related balance impairment, or neuropathy. Early-warning systems that flag these risks could create a window for intervention before complications set in.

World Brain Day Spotlight

The timing of this crisis coincides with World Brain Day on July 22, which the World Federation of Neurology has themed around equitable access to brain health care. The campaign's five pillars — equity, capability, visibility, protection, and advocacy — directly address the structural gaps India faces.

"Access to brain health is a profound global issue," said Professor David Dodick, co-chair of World Brain Day 2026. "While the disparity with low-income countries remains staggering, with 227 times fewer neurologists per capita, even in high-income countries, cost, primary care and specialist shortages, and overburdened systems prevent billions from receiving essential care."

For India's 1.4 billion people, closing that gap will require not just more neurologists, but a fundamentally different model of care — one where specialist knowledge reaches patients in their own districts rather than waiting for them to travel to a handful of overburdened city hospitals.
